paper_title: Relevance Does Not Imply Applicability: Experience Activation for Personal GUI Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Personal Graphical User Interface (GUI) agents rely on interaction history to infer what a user wants from ambiguous instructions and to anticipate recurring routines. Existing approaches retrieve task-relevant history and append it to the policy's context, implicitly assuming that experience relevant to a task remains useful for each decision within it. We find that this help is largely spent at the first decision: retrieved history strongly improves the opening step of an episode, yet provides little sustained benefit over the remaining 90\% of steps, and offers weak guidance on whether a proactive suggestion is warranted. A relevant record may tell the agent where to begin, but not which past action applies to the current screen or whether a routine is due now. The underlying issue is that relevance does not imply applicability}: relevance is determined at the task level, whereas applicability depends on the situation at decision time. We therefore recast personalization as experience activation and introduce ExpActivator, a training-free framework that activates only the experience applicable to the current situation. During execution, ExpActivator matches each new screen to historical states in the frozen GUI backbone's latent space and supplies the corresponding action as a reference. Before execution, it activates a recurring intent only when the current time and scenario provide sufficient support, and otherwise abstains. Across four GUI backbones, ExpActivator improves within-trajectory step success by 28\% on average, achieves the best personalized execution on every backbone while using about one-fifth as many history tokens, and reaches approximately 2.3$\times$ the Matthews correlation coefficient of the strongest proactive baseline. Experience pays where it is activated, not where it is appended.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Personal Graphical User Interface (GUI) agents operate apps on users own device, where much of what the user wants is never stated explicitly (Jang et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026). Order my usual coffee names neither the app, the drink, nor the store; user who orders coffee at home every morning may even expect the agent to offer it without being asked. Such gaps can only be filled from the users interaction history (Yang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026): in personalized execution, history helps resolve an ambiguous instruction and carry it out the way this user would; in proactive suggestion, it helps decide whether recurring routine is due before any instruction is given.1 The question is therefore not whether history helps, but when and how past experience should influence each decision. Figure 1: From retrieval to activation. Top: personalized execution. Bottom: proactive suggestion. (a) Retrieval supplies whole trajectories without indicating the matching step. (b) ExpActivator activates the matching step. (c) Retrieval returns related records without indicating whether routine is due. (d) ExpActivator activates the routine matching the time and scenario, then suggests or abstains. Existing personalized GUI agents primarily use history through task-level retrieval: they retrieve related records, profiles, or intent memories and append them to the policys context (Chai et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2025; Kong et al., 2026; Lyu et al., 2026). This implicitly treats task-level relevance as sufficient proxy 1Throughout the paper, task is user goal such as ordering coffee, an episode is one execution of task on the device, step is single screen within an episode together with the action taken on it, and routine is task that the user repeats at similar times and in similar scenarios, such as at home or while commuting. 1 for decision-level applicability: once experience is retrieved for task, the same context is expected to remain useful as subsequent decisions change. For execution, this leaves sharper question: not only how much retrieved history helps, but for how long. Our experiments reveal sharp limitation of task-level retrieval. In execution, retrieved history strongly improves the opening decision, which commits the agent to an application, yet provides little sustained benefit over the remaining 90% of steps. This is because the instruction stays fixed while the screen changes at every step. retrieved trajectory may indicate where to begin, but it does not tell the agent which past action fits this screen (Figure 1a). Proactive suggestion faces similar problem. The same routine may be retrieved both at 8 a.m. at home and during an evening commute, even though it is appropriate only in the former (Chen et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026; Nathani et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026). Even methods that organize routines by time and scenario (Lyu et al., 2026) still leave the policy to decide whether the routine applies. Both cases stem from gap between relevance and applicability. Retrieval identifies experience related to the task, whereas whether that experience applies depends on the situation at decision time. We therefore recast personalization as experience activation: retrieval narrows history to relevant candidates, while the situation at each decision activates the experience that applies. We instantiate this principle in ExpActivator, training-free framework operating at two granularities. During execution, the current screen activates the matching historical state in the frozen GUI backbones latent space, and its associated action is supplied as reference; the match is recomputed as the interface changes. Before execution, the current time and scenario determine whether recurring intent is sufficiently supported, and the agent abstains otherwise (Figure 1b,d). Personalization thus becomes decision-time selection problem rather than one-time retrieval problem. Across four GUI backbones, ExpActivator improves within-trajectory step success by 28% on average, achieves about 20% higher overall step success than the strongest baseline while using about one-fifth as many history tokens, and reaches approximately 2.3 its Matthews correlation coefficient for proactive suggestion. Controlled comparisons show that the same history helps substantially more when its applicable action is selected than when it is appended in full. Experience pays where it is activated, not where it is appended. Our contributions are as follows: diagnosis of task-level retrieval. We show that task-level relevance does not imply decisionlevel applicability. Retrieved history helps mainly at the opening step of an episode and offers weak guidance on when routine is due. Experience activation at two levels. We introduce ExpActivator, training-free framework with step-level and task-level activation. Step-level activation matches every new screen to historical state and uses its action as reference, while task-level activation suggests recurring intent only when the current time and scenario support it. Evidence for decision-time activation. Across four GUI backbones, step-level activation consistently improves personalized execution and task-level activation improves proactive suggestion, while using substantially less history context than existing approaches.

sections.title: 3 Experiment
sections.content: 3.1 Experimental Setup Dataset. We evaluate on AndroidIntent (Lyu et al., 2026), built from long-term mobile records of 82 users across 135 applications and 13 scenario categories. The chronological first 80% of each users records forms the history Mu (15,966 records), and the remaining episodes are evaluation targets excluded from retrieval. Personalized execution has 775 episodes with 7,915 steps whose instructions are deliberately ambiguous: request such as checking updates names neither application nor content, so the intended behavior must be recovered from history. Proactive suggestion has 315 states (215 positive, 100 negative), each giving only user, time, and scenario. Metrics. For execution we report action-type accuracy (Type), step success rate (SSR), and the benchmarks cumulative success rate (CSR). For proactive suggestion we report the official semantic score of emitted suggestions (Sem.), precision (P), balanced accuracy (BA), and the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), which is zero for any rule that cannot tell positive from negative states; recall, falsealarm rate, and F1 are listed in Appendix C.5. Comparisons use paired bootstrap resampling, and all configurations are calibrated on held-out history before evaluation (Appendix B). Backbones and baselines. We use four frozen open GUI backbones with different visual encoders and GUI training, Qwen3-VL-8B, MAI-UI-8B, Qwen3.5-9B, and GUI-Owl-1.5-8B, with the proprietary QwenVL-Max as an external reference. Within each backbone we compare ExpActivator with the history mechanisms of the benchmark: Recent supplies the latest records, Retrieve the records most similar to the instruction, LLM-UM an offline LLM-written profile, and HIM-Agent hierarchical intent memory (Lyu et al., 2026); Base uses no history. All methods read the same history and share model revisions and inference settings, so comparisons are paired step by step. 3.2 Main Results Personalized execution. Table 1 shows that ExpActivator achieves the best Type, SSR, and CSR on all four backbones, even though these backbones differ in visual encoder and GUI training. An episode opens with one decision that commits it to an application and then proceeds through trajectory of interface states, giving 775 openings and 7,140 subsequent actions. Scoring the two separately tests the question raised in Section 1: does retrieved record remain usable once the trajectory is under way? Retrieved experience is spent at the first decision. History matters most at the opening decision. On Qwen3-VL-8B, the strongest baselines raise it from 28.3% without history to 62.3%, and ExpActivator raises it to 70.1%  (Table 2)  . The pattern holds on every backbone, where no baseline adds more than 14% within the trajectory while ExpActivator adds 28% on average (Appendix F.2). Retrieval tells the agent which experience is related, and that answer is used up by the first decision; keeping experience useful afterwards requires selecting from it again at every observation. No evaluated baseline therefore matches it on accuracy and cost at once. The benefit also does not depend on long personal history. Selecting beats appending. To isolate the value of selection, we restrict the history to the single top-ranked trajectory and compare two ways of using it. Supplying the trajectory whole, as retrievalbased memories do, yields 18.5% SSR, on par with using no history at all. Letting step-level activation select one action from the same trajectory raises SSR to 23.8%, 29% relative improvement. The same experience therefore helps far more when the agent receives only the part that applies, which mirrors the within-trajectory failure of the memory baselines in Section 3.3. Refresh at every observation. Selecting the right step also requires selecting it at the right moment. Holding the eight retrieved trajectories fixed, we keep the matching rule but feed it stale screen. Matching against the previous screen lowers SSR by 15% relative, and refreshing the reference only every fourth step lowers it by 13%. Agreement between the selected reference and the recorded action drops even more sharply, by 38% relative, because stale screen activates step the user has already passed. Recomputing the match at every observation is therefore not refinement of the mechanism but the mechanism itself. Activation moves across trajectories. The refresh results imply that the activated reference should change as the interface changes, and Figure 4 shows that it does. On every backbone, about 92% of episodes draw their references from at least two past trajectories, 3.4 on average, and the reference moves to different trajectory on 55% of consecutive steps. No single past trajectory, however relevant, could supply these references on its own. Context gates the suggestion. Task-level activation relies on three contextual components, and removing each one hurts in distinct way. Without time weighting, BA falls by about 5% relative, since repetition alone does not reveal when routine applies. Without the scenario condition, BA falls by 11% relative and false alarms rise from 37% to 62%, so scenario agreement is what keeps activation selective. Frequency normalization leaves every trigger decision unchanged but improves the semantic quality of emitted suggestions by 4% relative, by favoring routines that match the context on each occurrence rather than on few. Time decides when to fire, scenario decides whether to fire, and frequency decides what to say. 3.5 Case Study Figure 5 shows both granularities of activation on real records. On the left, each current screen of NUS NextBus task activates recorded state that nearly duplicates it, and the reference moves from one past trip to another as the screens change, following the trip that matches the current stage of the task (Appendix G). Before dawn and shortly after 1 p.m., no routine has enough support and ExpActivator stays silent. Figures 12 and 11 show the same behavior for five more users.

sections.title: 4 Related Work
sections.content: Personalized GUI Agents. Personalized GUI benchmarks evaluate whether agents follow user preferences across mobile tasks, with settings ranging from recorded demonstrations to interactive preference elicitation (Yang et al., 2025; Nie et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025). Methods use preference learning and hierarchical memory to recover information omitted from instructions (Wang et al., 2026; Lyu et al., 2026). The closest precedent, PersonalAlign, introduces AndroidIntent and HIM-Agent, which aggregates long-term records into preference and routine prototypes (Lyu et al., 2026). ExpActivator extends this focus on recovering user intent to selecting the historical behavior that can guide each decision. It distinguishes retrieving task-relevant trajectory from identifying the historical step appropriate for the current screen. Memory and Experience Reuse in GUI Agents. Reusable workflows and structured memories provide experience for GUI planning and action generation (Wang et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2026; Qin et al., 2026; Chung et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025). Memory can also be refreshed or selectively managed during execution (Zhu et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026). MementoGUI learns multimodal memory selection and compression with frozen GUI backbone (Zeng et al., 2026), while ATMem tracks the role and status of task information and learns selective memory use (Liu et al., 2026). ExpActivator contributes mechanism for selecting concrete actions from personal history without training memory 8 controller or the GUI policy. Step-level activation matches each screen against historical states within task-relevant trajectories and updates the action reference after every observation. The frozen policy combines this reference with the current screen and execution history to produce the action. Controlled comparisons with fixed candidate history support the value of screen matching and reference updates for personalized action prediction. Proactive Assistance. Proactive mobile benchmarks study how user history, screen activity, and device context support intent inference without explicit requests (Yang et al., 2025; Chai et al., 2026; Kong et al., 2026). Interactive evaluations further examine intervention timing and responses to feedback (Chen et al., 2026; Nathani et al., 2026). Closest to our setting, HIM-Agent uses temporal and scenario regularities to organize routine memory and supplies representative intents and states for proactive reasoning (Lyu et al., 2026). ExpActivator uses this contextual information in an explicit activation rule applied before suggestion generation. Task-level activation separates the support required to consider routine from the contextual score used to rank it, and abstains when no routine qualifies. ExpActivator provides common basis for using personal history across execution and suggestion: current conditions select an action or intent reference, while the frozen backbone generates the response. Both thus adapt their use of experience without fine-tuning.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We have argued that personal experience helps only where it is activated: relevant trajectory need not contain an action suited to the current screen, and familiar routine may become due even without any instruction. ExpActivator acts on this principle without any training. Step-level activation re-anchors the action reference to every observation, while task-level activation fires only when time and scenario support routine. The same record store then yields, across four frozen backbones, the best personalized execution and the only selective proactive suggestion among the evaluated methods, at the lowest history-token cost. For personal agents, the lesson is compact: experience pays where it is activated, not where it is appended.

Every target execution episode is excluded from execution retrieval. Proactive queries contain user identity, time, and scenario; records with the exact query timestamp are excluded from routine membership as in Section 2.3. Historical calibration fixes retrieval neighborhood sizes, descriptor layouts, and centering statistics before policy evaluation. The semantic encoders, visual towers, application-label compiler, and GUI policies remain frozen. Ht in Section 2.2 is the benchmarks preceding action sequence. Reference selection uses the current instruction and screen, while the current target action is reserved for scoring. Appendix details the step-level activation experiments on selecting versus appending and on reference updates, followed by the task-level activation experiments on time, scenario, and frequency normalization. C.3 Metric Definitions Execution. For predicted action (cid:98)at and the recorded action at, type accuracy counts (cid:98)at as correct when the action types agree. Step success additionally requires the arguments to agree: click or long click must fall within normalized distance of 0.14 of the target on 1000 1000 grid, scroll must share the direction, typed text must reach character similarity of 0.7, and an application opening must name the target application; back, home, wait, and finish match on type alone. SSR averages step success over all steps. The benchmarks cumulative success rate weights the steps of an episode of length by CSR = k<Le k<Le (Le) me,k (Le) , (L) = e0.6k k<L e0.6k , (10) where me,k {0, 1} is step success at position of episode e. CSR therefore emphasizes the early decisions that determine whether personalized episode starts on the right path. Proactive suggestion. method emits suggestion or abstains on each state. With true and false positives and negatives counted over the 315 states, precision is = TP/(TP + FP), recall is = TP/(TP + FN), the false-alarm rate is FA = FP/(FP + TN), and BA = 1 2 (R + 1 FA). The Matthews correlation coefficient is MCC = TP TN FP FN (cid:112)(TP + FP)(TP + FN)(TN + FP)(TN + FN) , (11) which is zero for rule that suggests on every state and, unlike F1, is not inflated by the 68% share of positive states. The semantic score follows the benchmark: for every suggestion emitted on positive state it averages the normalized edit similarity and the Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B cosine similarity between the suggestion and the recorded intent, and Sem. reports the mean over these suggestions. Statistical comparison. Every comparison is paired, since all methods are evaluated on the same steps or states. We resample users with replacement, keep all of resampled users steps or states together, and recompute the metric difference on each of 20,000 draws; difference is called significant when its 95% percentile interval excludes zero. C.4 Baseline Construction All baselines read the same chronological history as ExpActivator and are inserted through the native prompt of each backbone. Recent supplies the latest three records with their intent, application, and actions. Retrieve supplies the three same-user records whose intents are most similar to the instruction under Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B. sections.content: D.1 Step-level Activation: Selecting versus Appending Protocol. We use the existing history split, retrieval scores, and history-calibrated visual representation without additional parameter tuning. For each test episode we fix the highest-ranked usable trajectory retrieved from that users historical pool. The Whole trajectory condition supplies this trajectory as complete record, and the Selected reference condition applies step-level activation (Section 2.2) to the same trajectory and supplies one action. Both run the frozen Qwen3-VL-8B policy on the 7,140 within-trajectory actions with the current screen and the ground-truth preceding actions visible. second control, at Kξ = 8, replaces the selected reference with the action immediately preceding it in the same historical trajectory. Intervals resample the 82 users with replacement 20,000 times, and inference uses greedy decoding with seed 0, maximum context length of 8,192 tokens, and up to 256 output tokens. Results. Threshold Sensitivity of Task-level Activation Task-level activation declares six constants: the routine threshold η, the minimum total support nmin, the minimum same-scenario support nctx, the temporal bandwidth σ, the activation threshold δ, and the normalization exponent γ. This section re-runs the activation rule of Section 2.3 over the sealed routine index for grids of these constants, so the reported operating point can be read against the surface it sits on. Only activation is re-run: no suggestion is generated and no model is called. The reimplementation reproduces the sealed run exactly at the declared setting (AUROC 80.37, balanced accuracy 72.66, recall 82.33, false alarms 37.00), which is asserted before any sweep. The sweeps are diagnostic: every reported result uses the declared constants. Routine threshold and minimum support. Over η [0.88, 0.98] and nmin 12, activation AUROC stays above 75 in all 40 cells and varies by less than 5.4 points (Figure 7); the declared setting (η, nmin) = (0.94, 12) reaches 80.37, within 0.33 points of the grid maximum, so the operating point sits on broad 19 plateau rather than sharp peak. Beyond nmin = 12 the surface falls away, to 73.24 at nmin = 16 and 58.95 at nmin = 24. This is coverage effect rather than an instability of the score: requiring that many repetitions leaves progressively more states with no eligible routine at all, rising from 27.6% at nmin = 12 to 41.9% at 16 and 73.0% at 24, and those states receive the constant abstention score, which removes the discrimination the metric measures.
